html:
The Battle of Malplaquet was fought on 11 September 1709 near the village of Malplaquet in northern France, close to today's border with Belgium. The allied army of the Duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene of Savoy drove a French army under Marshal Villars from the field, but at a terrible cost.

It came late in the War of the Spanish Succession. After a hard winter and failed peace talks, the allies wanted to break through the French border forts and march on Paris. Villars moved to block them and dug in between two woods with about 75,000 men. The allies, with about 86,000, attacked both wings for hours and at last broke the centre. The French pulled back in good order. The allies lost over 20,000 men, about twice the French loss. The Dutch infantry suffered worst.

The allies took the fortress of Mons, but they could not invade France. It was one of the bloodiest battles of the 18th century. The losses shocked Britain, where a new government dismissed Marlborough in 1711 and looked for peace. Louis XIV kept his army and got better terms at the Peace of Utrecht in 1713.
